# Pattern Transferability and Generalization {#sec-loop-patterns-across-stack}

::: {.epigraph}
> "There is no single development, in either technology or in management technique, that by itself promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity."
>
> — Frederick P. Brooks Jr., *No Silver Bullet* [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet, p. 10]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What can be reused across architecture problems, what must be adapted, and what must be re-established?*

**Core thesis:** *Cross-problem transfer requires identifying invariant principles, accounting for distribution shift across workloads and technologies, and recognizing when prior claims must be re-qualified.*
:::

A new chip program rarely starts from nothing. It inherits register-transfer level (RTL) modules, simulation scripts, learned surrogate models, and records of earlier trade-offs, and each of them was qualified under conditions the new program may not share. A systolic array shape tuned on dense matrix tiles, or a congestion predictor fitted to one process library, keeps producing confident answers after those conditions change. When workloads shift from dense matrix multiplication to sparse attention, when instruction set architectures (ISAs) gain vector extensions, or when physical implementation migrates from FinFET to nanosheet transistors, prior architectural conclusions can stop holding without any warning from the artifacts that encode them. An optimal cache line size or systolic array aspect ratio derived for one workload can become a bottleneck under another.

The difficulty is that reuse is rarely all or nothing. A simulator wrapper may carry forward unchanged while the conclusion it once supported no longer answers the new question, and a team that must either accept or rebuild the whole package pays for the mistake in one direction or the other. The chapter therefore separates what moves from what stays attached to its source conditions (@fig-ch09-cover-map), and asks what evidence a carried component needs before it can steer a new decision.

![**Reusable architectural components transfer across designs while empirical conclusions remain bounded to source evidence.** Reusable units from a source study record (data, representations, methods, tool interfaces, and configurations) are isolated and assigned explicit target actions (carry, update, replace, or retire). Target-grounded checks validate new design decisions while the original conclusion remains attached to its source conditions. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/ch09-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch09-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which a source record meets a changed condition, after which units are carried, updated, replaced, or retired and target claims are checked anew."}

## Foundations of Cross-Design Architectural Transfer {#sec-foundations-cross-design-transfer}

Reusing prior design work can save engineering time, but risks carrying forward obsolete assumptions that invalidate new decisions. The operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers change what a reusable pattern looks like, because each layer leaves different decisions open.

1. **Layer 1 patterns.** Point assistance generates or checks an isolated artifact inside a frozen architecture, such as a peripheral register block, a unit testbench, or SystemVerilog assertions for an existing cache controller. Such a pattern transfers conditionally, and remains valid only while the local interface contracts and timing invariants it assumed still hold. Because the assistance sees nothing outside its artifact, a changed neighbor requires integration work and fresh equivalence checks.
2. **Layer 2 patterns.** Search inside a fixed container $\Theta$ tunes parameters such as systolic array dimensions, cache capacities, buffer depths, or macro coordinates. The search method or surrogate can move to a new target, but the tuned configuration $\theta^* \in \Theta$ does not. Re-optimizing inside the target container can also improve a local proxy while moving cost outside the container, a trap examined later in this chapter.
3. **Layer 3 patterns.** An AI-native design system would revisit decisions across abstraction boundaries rather than inside one template. What could transfer at that layer is the specification contract, the verification harness, and the procedure for co-adapting hardware and software, not a frozen microarchitecture. Each regenerated design would still owe its own target checks.

Prior architectural artifacts fall into core principles, conditional modules, and empirical performance conclusions, each of which fails to transfer in a different way: a principle travels broadly whenever its framing assumptions match the target, whereas a hardware module or tool wrapper survives only while its interface invariants hold, and an empirical performance conclusion stays attached to the source evidence that supported it.

Because hardware behavior depends on compiler scheduling, memory semantics, wire parasitics, and power delivery, an unchanged RTL module can behave differently in a new environment and a learned surrogate may stop predicting the property its caller expects. Transferring an architectural pattern to a new target therefore begins with a dependency audit that identifies which relations need checking before reuse.

The transfer test proposed here opens with an admission check that compares the source and target decisions before running four stages (@fig-transfer-test-flow). Whenever candidate boundaries, optimization objectives, constraints, acceptance criteria, comparator rules, or error costs have shifted, the decision itself reopens because numerical recalibration alone cannot establish that a prior conclusion answers a changed question; the four stages still apply, but they now support a new design problem.

1. **Partition the source into transfer units.** Separate the source record into data, representations, methods, tool interfaces, checks, and configurations. Keep each empirical conclusion linked to the evidence and conditions that supported it.
2. **Isolate the affected slice.** Trace which dependencies and invariants the target workload, ISA, or process shift may have changed, distinguishing known violations from relations that still need checking.
3. **Assign target actions.** Designate each unit to be carried forward, updated, retrained, recalibrated, replaced, or retired.
4. **Enforce target checks and test the transfer benefit.** Requalify affected units against target references and compare decision quality and total cost with a matched target-only baseline, including the cost of adaptation and requalification.

![**Transfer testing partitions prior engineering records without porting unverified source conclusions.** An initial admission check evaluates decision compatibility, followed by four stages that isolate affected dependencies, assign unit actions (carry, update, replace, or retire), and enforce target checks on changed interfaces. Unaffected components carry forward while dependent claims are selectively reopened for target validation. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-transfer-test-flow){#fig-transfer-test-flow width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram of transfer testing, beginning at the source record, whose artifacts, methods, checks, and supported conclusion feed four stage boxes: transfer units separating data, methods, checks, and dependencies; changed dependencies tracing each material change to dependent claims and interfaces; target actions to carry, update, replace, or retire each unit; and target checks on affected units and every interface with a changed neighbor. The flow ends in a target decision box where a new comparison over target measurements supports a new conclusion. A supporting band states that components may move while the source conclusion stays attached to its source conditions and limits."}

Consider a compiler upgrade that changes one lowering pass, such as how a fused attention kernel is tiled onto an accelerator's scratchpad. The RTL of the accelerator is untouched, so its functional-equivalence results still hold. The kernel's measured latency and bandwidth were produced through the old lowering, so those performance claims reopen, and the interface between the compiler's output and the accelerator's command queue needs an integration check because one side of it changed. Everything else in the source record keeps its support. When the admission check confirms that the design question is unchanged, this is the saving the staging buys, since only the claims downstream of the changed pass need new target evidence before any candidate enters the commitment comparison.

The case for reusing an engineering artifact depends on how completely its dependency map captures what changed and whether target checks cover the affected claims and interfaces. In a learned macro-placement policy trained on one family of floorplans, for example, a process migration can alter metal routing resources and reshape the relationship between macro coordinates and downstream congestion. Although the policy might still offer a useful starting point, its source performance cannot settle that question until requalification compares its predictions or placement choices against extracted target results to establish where it can safely guide the new search.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Transfer components, not conclusions"}
**The principle:** When adapting prior design work to new workloads, process nodes, or constraints, artifacts, tool paths, and intermediate data may carry forward, but a source conclusion does not carry forward until the conditions that supported it are shown to hold in the target.

**The application:** Before relying on a prior architectural conclusion, check whether its supporting conditions still hold in the target. Changed or uncertain dependencies require new evidence; unaffected claims can retain their source support.
:::

## Target System Shifts and Decision Reopening {#sec-target-shifts-decision-reopening}

A target system shift reopens prior architectural decisions whenever new workloads, silicon constraints, or interface contracts break the assumptions behind the original problem formulation. A *design problem* is the complete decision context that gives alternatives their meaning; it explicitly names candidate boundaries, target workloads, software stacks, constraints, credible comparators, and error costs. Benchmarks supply workloads, candidates represent design points, and tools observe properties, but none of these carries the full decision context in isolation. Comparing source and target determines whether the study answers the same question under changed conditions or addresses a different architecture question.

Target system changes fall into three categories.

- **Distributional transfer.** The objective, legal actions, artifact boundary, and acceptance criteria remain stable, while the workload, operating conditions, or candidate population shift within that space. Examples include shifting batch sizes or input frame rates while keeping CPU ISA vector extensions or Triton compiler intermediate representation (IR) constant. A larger shift of the same kind occurs when AI workloads move from dense general matrix multiply (GEMM) kernels toward sparse attention or mixture-of-experts (MoE) token routing. Operational intensity can fall and token-dependent routing can make work irregular, so an array shape chosen for dense tiles may lose utilization; whether it must change depends on batching, mapping, and the memory system.
- **Component or integration transfer.** The core decision remains stable while differences emerge in a component, interface, tool, library, or process condition along the executable or measurement path, such as updating a compiler backend, remapping a kernel from Arm Scalable Vector Extension operations to Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) tile operations,[^fn-amx-tiles-c09] or altering neural processing unit (NPU) tensor dataflows. Because migrating from FinFET to gate-all-around nanosheets alters device and wire resistance and capacitance (RC) parasitics, whereas moving from a monolithic die to 2.5D/3D chiplets joined by Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) introduces die-to-die crossings with their own latency and energy costs, floorplanning heuristics and wirelength surrogates calibrated on monolithic dies cannot account for those crossings until target evidence requalifies their congestion and latency predictions across the multi-die package and verifies each path's lowering and interface assumptions.
- **New design problem.** The objective, legal actions, artifact boundary, or acceptance criteria change fundamentally (such as transitioning from datacenter throughput under a 700\ W-class accelerator envelope to a strict 3\ W mobile or headset thermal limit).

[^fn-amx-tiles-c09]: **Intel AMX tile operations**: Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) departs from conventional one-dimensional vector lanes by introducing eight two-dimensional tile registers of up to 1\ KiB each and matrix multiply-accumulate instructions (such as `TDPBF16PS`). Lowering a kernel to AMX requires the compiler to block the computation into 2D tiles and to load an explicit tile configuration (`LDTILECFG`) before use, which changes register-allocation assumptions and adds a large architectural state that the operating system must save on context switches.

These distinctions apply claim by claim and dependency by dependency, not uniformly across the target. A single target change often combines these forms across distinct architectural dependencies. Selective requalification handles claims affected by distributional or component changes, whereas a new design problem forces reopening every claim tied to the changed question. The raw magnitude of a change does not dictate the response; a large workload shift may remain within the same design problem, whereas a single-line modification to an objective or action space can create a new one. Treating every workload adjustment as a new design problem wastes effort on checks whose assumptions still hold; treating a changed objective as parameter drift can preserve a conclusion that no longer answers the question.

Whether a change is material therefore depends on the specific claim and the dependency path that supports it: updating a compiler toolchain reopens executable performance claims without touching RTL functional equivalence, whereas shifting a library operating corner reopens timing and power closure without invalidating compiler-semantics results. In general, a change is material to a claim whenever it alters the candidate identity, executable path, measured quantity, objective, decision rule, ranking, constraint verdict, or underlying physical mechanism.

Every qualified component carries a *support region* (the joint set of workload, design-family, tool, library, process, interface, and version conditions under which it was originally verified). A source-to-target shift emerges whenever work qualified in one region is applied to another. @sec-feedback-verification-trust introduced a distribution shift as a change in the workloads, tool versions, or operating conditions that generated the data a surrogate or claim was qualified on [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift], and drift as such a change observed over time. In architectural systems those conditions include software stacks, compilers, libraries, process calibrations, and hardware interfaces, so a shift can reach a claim through its executable or measurement path even when the inputs a learned model sees look unchanged.

Within this protocol, generalization measures performance on unseen cases drawn from declared target conditions, whereas transfer tests reuse after a material shift from source to target,[^fn-transfer-c09] and robustness (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect) measures stability under named perturbations, faults, or attacks. The distribution-shift and requalification analysis in @sec-feedback-verification-trust then determines when previously qualified evidence requires fresh target checks.

[^fn-transfer-c09]: **Generalization vs. transfer**: In this test protocol, generalization evaluates model accuracy on held-out tasks drawn from the same underlying data distribution, whereas transfer evaluates performance retention after a material shift in workload semantics, ISA extensions, toolchain version, or physical process parameters. A study must state its source and target conditions and which changes it evaluates before either term supports an architecture claim.


Standard dataset-shift tests compare reference samples against incoming data to report divergence [@RabanserEtAl2019FailingLoudly]. In architectural evaluation, a detected shift reopens the affected support claim at once, but because the statistical signal indicates only that the data moved without explaining why, it does not authorize automated adaptation; the architect still needs explicit dependency analysis and target checks to resolve it.

The preliminary spatial array experiment introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust shows where those lines fall in practice. Evaluating five systolic array shapes in SCALE-Sim [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3] on a synthetic three-layer general matrix multiply (GEMM) slice is a Layer 2 parameter search that sweeps array aspect ratios within a fixed structural template $\Theta$ against an uncalibrated cycle-and-utilization proxy. Under that local metric, the source study found a tie and retained the 32 by 32 reference array, a no-change finding that remains confined to its synthetic source context.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Inline values for the transposition probe, read from the retained study record:
#   data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json
# Score S = total cycles / (average layer utilization as a fraction), lower is better;
# the margin is the loser's score minus the winner's, as a share of the loser's score.
import json as _json9t
from pathlib import Path as _Path9t
import _python.plots as _ap9t

_study9t = _json9t.loads(
    (_Path9t(_ap9t.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "ai_systolic_array_study"
     / "recorded" / "reference" / "study_results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
_probe9t = {e["candidate_id"]: e["metrics"] for e in _study9t["evaluations"] if e["arm"] == "mechanism_probe"}


def _score9t(cid):
    m = _probe9t[cid]
    return m["total_cycles"] / (m["avg_layer_util_pct"] / 100)


def _margin9t(winner, loser):
    return 100 * (_score9t(loser) - _score9t(winner)) / _score9t(loser)


_orig9t = _margin9t("probe_original_16x64", "probe_original_64x16")
_trans9t = _margin9t("probe_transposed_16x64", "probe_transposed_64x16")
_mc9t = _study9t["mechanism_claim"]
assert abs(_orig9t - _mc9t["original_margin_pct"]) < 1e-9
assert abs(_trans9t - _mc9t["transposed_margin_pct"]) < 1e-9
assert _mc9t["observed_original_winner"] == _mc9t["observed_transposed_winner"] == "16x64"
tp_orig_margin = f"{_orig9t:.1f}"
tp_trans_margin = f"{_trans9t:.1f}"
tp_ratio = f"{_orig9t / _trans9t:.1f}"
```

The same record also holds the book's one measured instance of a conclusion meeting a shift, where the mechanism probe of @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization ran the $16 \times 64$ and $64 \times 16$ arrays on both the original workload and a transposed version with $M$ and $N$ swapped. Although the $16 \times 64$ array scored `{python} tp_orig_margin`% better than the $64 \times 16$ array on the original workload and still won after transposition, its lead shrank to `{python} tp_trans_margin`%, so the ranking survived the distributional shift while its magnitude did not. A team that carried forward the source margin, for instance to decide whether the wide array was worth its extra modeled write traffic, would have relied on a margin `{python} tp_ratio` times larger than what the transposed workload actually supports. Because the probe evaluates a single synthetic three-layer workload under a deterministic simulator while changing several factors at once, this narrow test demonstrates that a performance margin need not transfer rather than estimating how much margins typically shrink.

For a Lighthouse design considering this array as one candidate compute organization, an implementation commitment asks a different question.

> Should the 32 by 32 array, together with its compiler-visible tiling and
> memory-interface contract, be frozen for RTL implementation in the
> Lighthouse subsystem?

Because this question alters the artifact boundary, acceptance criteria, and consequences of error, it creates a new design problem that a parameter search inside the frozen template cannot answer. The isolated simulator score cannot establish whether the array and its memory system can serve the Lighthouse workload within a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope, whereas freezing an interface constrains compiler tiling, static random-access memory (SRAM) banking, interconnect traffic, and power delivery. If off-chip memory traffic turned out to dominate the power budget, a sweep within template $\Theta$ could not alter the interface or repartition memory; resolving that bottleneck would mean reopening the interface itself. The retained source record contains none of those target results, leaving the transfer application later in this chapter to specify the work still required.

## Decoupling Transfer Units Across System Boundaries {#sec-decoupling-transfer-units}

Hardware, software, and tools evolve at different rates, so a team partitions a source system before moving it rather than transferring it whole. Data, state, methods, tools, checks, and conclusions rarely share a single lifetime in an architecture project, and treating them as an indivisible package forces a choice between copying everything blindly and rebuilding the infrastructure entirely. Naming the units separately is what makes a source-to-target comparison actionable, because each unit can then carry its own dependency and its own check.

### Automated Dependency Mapping and Invariant Extraction {#sec-automated-dependency-mapping}

Every transfer unit carries an *invariant* (a core relation that must remain true across both source and target for the unit to retain its meaning), whether stated explicitly in interface specifications or left implicit in the implementation. As an untested capability, this book proposes that an AI-native design system combine execution logs, source analysis, and environment metadata into a dependency graph that flags assumptions a target change might break. Because such a graph remains incomplete wherever the source record omitted a dependency, reviewers must first identify the units and claims affected by known dependency changes independently and verify that the generated map reaches them; while recovering those known cases supports using the map without proving completeness, any miss requires correcting the graph and widening the requalification scope.

Consider an illustrative cache controller that consumes SRAM data two cycles after issuing a request. A target macro that returns data after three cycles breaks that fixed-latency invariant unless the controller implements a ready/valid handshake or credit-based flow control.[^fn-flow-control-c09] While static analysis and a generated SystemVerilog assertion could help expose the mismatch, the verification task is to confirm that the assertion captures the intended request–response behavior, that the target macro model represents the changed latency, and that the property is genuinely exercised. Environmental assumptions (`assume property`) for macro driving signals require separate scrutiny because missing constraints can admit behaviors the real environment cannot produce, whereas overly restrictive assumptions or unreachable property antecedents let a check pass vacuously. A failed check blocks reuse of the controller under its old timing assumption, while a passing generated assertion confirms only the checked relation rather than proving that every implicit timing assumption has been uncovered.

[^fn-flow-control-c09]: **Credit-based flow control**: A flow-control mechanism where the sender tracks available buffer slots in the receiver using a credit counter, decrementing on transmit and incrementing upon receiving return credit tokens. Unlike ready/valid handshakes, which introduce combinational backpressure paths that can limit operating frequency across long wires, credit-based flow control allows the link to be pipelined across long wires and, when the receiver buffer covers the round-trip latency, to stream without stall bubbles.

A transfer unit is best scoped to the smallest versioned boundary that has a declared interface or invariant and an independently meaningful target check. A dependency that no such check can isolate stays in the same unit, since splitting it off would leave nothing to verify it. Consider an LLVM IR module lowered through a backend supporting RISC-V Vector (RVV) or x86 AVX-512, or a Triton kernel compiled for a separately declared, supported target. The compiler toolchain and generated binary can be treated as separate units only when their identities and inputs are fixed and the binary receives an independent check for the claimed property, such as semantic equivalence for behavior or an application binary interface (ABI) check for interface compatibility. Otherwise, the compiler-to-binary lowering path must be transferred and checked together.

The transfer map puts the four stages into practice, naming the action a broken dependency permits and the target check that action requires (@tbl-ch9-transfer-map). The configured-system row is the one most easily missed. It reopens even when the configuration itself is untouched, because a neighbor it depends on has changed. Each action pairs with a domain-specific check on held-out tasks or hardware references; the resulting evidence supports reuse only within the conditions and properties checked. For learned components, *held-out* means target tasks kept apart from fitting or calibration.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data, records, and current knowledge** | Workload, design space, objectives, provenance, collection conditions, specifications, manuals, libraries, or project documents differ. | Reuse the historical record; refresh target data and sources; retire stale sources; narrow unsupported coverage. | Check trace and artifact provenance, source identity and version, target coverage and exclusions, source-to-target overlap, and whether retrieved material supports the target fact. |
| **Representation and project state** | Constraints, interfaces, artifact versions, or cross-layer relationships differ. | Refresh live state; adapt the representation; replace a representation that hides a required relationship. | Check schema and constraint completeness, version consistency, and integration with neighboring state. |
| **Learned component** | Training support, inputs, outputs, objectives, constraints, project facts, or data-generating conditions changed. | Requalify the unchanged component; rerun a generator or optimizer; recalibrate a numerical mapping; adapt, retrain, replace, or retire the component when needed. | Test every role it fills on held-out target tasks, including accuracy or calibration, candidate legality, objective quality, stale knowledge, failure classes, and performance against the declared comparator. |
| **Conventional method** | Analytical assumptions, solver formulation, design space, or objective changed. | Reuse, adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the method. | Check its assumptions on the target and compare its target result with the same decision rule used for other methods. |
| **Tool interface and environment component** | Command syntax, parameter meaning, output schema, status codes, tool or library version, constraint and configuration files, random seed, license, runtime, machine resource, reset behavior, or isolation changed. | Refresh configuration; adapt, replace, or retire the component; rerun affected work. | Check target-version execution, interface parsing and failure classification, constraints and stochastic state, reset and isolation behavior, resource accounting, and integration with connected tools. |
| **Empirical screening check** | Target coverage, observed conditions, error tolerance, or relationship to the target reference changed. | Requalify before reuse; recalibrate only when a numerical mapping or threshold changes; adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the check. | Measure target support and class-specific errors against a separate reference capable of observing the property at risk. |
| **Formal, equivalence, deterministic, or rule-based check** | The target specification, assumptions, properties, representation relation, rules, or tool version changed. | Review the specification mapping; requalify the target setup; adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the check. | Check property and assumption coverage, the relation being established, target tool integration, and known positive, negative, and inconclusive cases. |
| **Routing or escalation policy** | Check cost, consequence, qualified coverage, or available review capacity changed. | Adapt, replace, narrow, or retire the policy. | Exercise routing thresholds, uncertain cases, failure injection, escalation, and resource limits on the target. |
| **Configured system** | Any neighboring component or interface changed, even when this configuration did not. | Rerun target integration; recompose, adapt, replace, narrow, or reject the configuration when required. | Repeat the end-to-end target task with pinned versions, total product-path costs, failures, and a credible alternative. |
| **Architecture and contribution conclusions** | The target decision, comparator, budget, or measured path differs from the source. | Narrow the conclusion to its supported source scope or reject its transfer. | Repeat the architecture comparison and the matched contribution comparison under target conditions. |
: **Transfer decisions are component-specific.** A unit moves only by assigning an action suited to the broken dependency, paired with a target check observing the resulting architectural risk. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-map tbl-colwidths="[20,28,24,28]"}

A conclusion is never updated mechanically; it is narrowed to the conditions the target still satisfies or rejected outright, and rejection preserves the historical record while keeping stale evidence out of the new decision.

*Negative transfer* occurs when a transferred or adapted method performs worse on the target than a clean target-only alternative [@WangEtAl2019NegativeTransfer]. In computer architecture, evaluating negative transfer requires comparing overall decision quality and total methodology cost. A team that claims a transfer benefit needs a matched target-only comparison in which both arms receive identical tasks, budgets, and stopping rules, with the target-only arm starting without source priors. Both arms need comparable opportunities to tune on the target; an untuned target-only baseline can make reuse appear beneficial. Total cost accounting must include adaptation, requalification, and integration overhead alongside execution time, including physical checks when the target claim requires them.

Transfer also needs an economic justification. While partitioning a source record, tracing dependencies, requalifying carried units, and integrating them with changed neighbors all consume engineering effort, a fresh target study incurs its own costs to rebuild tools and collect data that the source may already provide. Reopening the architecture decision therefore does not settle whether reuse is worthwhile, because a source conclusion may no longer apply even while its simulator wrapper or workload-processing code remains expensive to reproduce.

The practical comparison weighs adaptation and requalification costs against rebuilding costs at comparable decision quality. Before committing the full budget, a limited transfer study can estimate which units are worth carrying, after which the matched target-only arm tests the claimed benefit. Source priors that worsen the decision or cost more than they save should be retired, whereas qualified tools and historical records can still carry forward; starting without a source prior is a defensible outcome that need not mean starting without reusable infrastructure.

### Isolating Design Slices {#sec-isolating-design-slices}

Dependency tracking isolates the affected slice of a configured system so the team can requalify claims that depend on changed conditions and run targeted integration checks wherever affected components meet unchanged neighbors. Because an incomplete dependency map can miss part of that slice, invariant extraction requires the independent verification checks described above. An NPU tensor dataflow shift (such as moving from weight-stationary to output-stationary tile scheduling)[^fn-output-stationary-c09] illustrates the boundary: it forces re-evaluating timing and memory power without altering compiler-level language semantics.

[^fn-output-stationary-c09]: **Output-stationary dataflow**: An accelerator dataflow where partial-sum accumulations remain stationary within the processing element registers until full reduction completes. This minimizes memory write traffic and accumulator power for large matrix tiles, inverting bandwidth and buffering demands relative to a weight-stationary schedule where weights remain pinned while activations and partial sums stream.

Target actions also differ by unit type: retraining modifies a learned component, recalibration adjusts a numerical mapping or threshold, data and representations are refreshed, and a tool interface may be reconfigured, adapted, or replaced. In a congestion predictor trained on prior routed designs, for example, the learned weights and feature schemas form the transferable artifact while placed netlists and process libraries supply the target inputs; checking schema compatibility and class-specific error bounds on held-out routed target designs then determines whether the unchanged weights suffice or require further adaptation.

Machine-learning work on distribution shift and hidden dependencies [@WangEtAl2019NegativeTransfer; @QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift; @SculleyEtAl2015Hidden] motivates checking interactions as well as individual components. A subsystem optimized in isolation can impose new costs on the system it joins. In hardware, those costs may appear in global interconnect and clock distribution, outside the boundary of the block-level report.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# Guard for @tbl-integration-overhead: the table cells must match the retained
# SCALE-Sim returns in data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json.
import json
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_study = json.loads(
    (
        _root / "data" / "studies" / "ai_systolic_array_study" / "recorded"
        / "reference" / "study_results.json"
    ).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
_metrics = {e["candidate_id"]: e["metrics"] for e in _study["evaluations"]}
_base = _metrics["conventional_baseline_32x32"]
_wide = _metrics["ai_wide_16x64"]
assert _base["total_cycles"] == _wide["total_cycles"] == 13917
assert round(_base["avg_layer_util_pct"], 1) == round(_wide["avg_layer_util_pct"], 1) == 41.2
assert (_base["sram_accesses"], _wide["sram_accesses"]) == (491520, 593920)
assert round(100 * (_wide["sram_accesses"] / _base["sram_accesses"] - 1), 1) == 20.8
assert _base["dram_reads"] == _wide["dram_reads"] == 129024
assert (_base["dram_writes"], _wide["dram_writes"]) == (204863, 409726)
assert round(_wide["dram_writes"] / _base["dram_writes"], 1) == 2.0
```

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="Container optimization can hide system cost"}
**The trap.** In a parameter search inside a fixed template, an automated exploration engine optimizes parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ within a fixed structural container against a local proxy metric, and a local win or tie is read as a system-level result.

**The mechanism.** In the retained systolic array study (@tbl-integration-overhead), a wider $16 \times 64$ geometry ties the $32 \times 32$ baseline on the score's cycle count (13,917, excluding prefetch) and on the local score, yet SCALE-Sim reports twice as many modeled DRAM-word writes (409,726 against 204,863) and more SRAM accesses [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. The container holds the memory interface and dataflow fixed, and the score never sees that traffic. The run did not model DRAM timing or energy, so the difference exposes a question the local score cannot answer rather than a measured system penalty.

| Returned quantity | $32 \times 32$ baseline | $16 \times 64$ candidate | Difference |
|:---|---:|---:|:---|
| Cycles excluding prefetch | 13,917 | 13,917 | Tied |
| Average layer utilization | 41.2% | 41.2% | Tied |
| Modeled SRAM accesses | 491,520 | 593,920 | $+20.8\%$ |
| Modeled DRAM-word reads | 129,024 | 129,024 | Identical |
| Modeled DRAM-word writes | 204,863 | 409,726 | $2.0\times$ |
: **A tied local score conceals a doubling of modeled write traffic.** Retained SCALE-Sim returns for the two tied candidates in the systolic array study. The scored cycle field excludes prefetch, so the tie does not establish equal end-to-end latency. Traffic counts are idealized word counts (no DRAM timing model) and carry no energy or power estimate [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. {#tbl-integration-overhead tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

**The lesson.** Bound such searches and transfer checks to the smallest enclosing boundary that captures interconnect, memory traffic, and thermal coupling, and report what the local score omits. When a quantity outside the container decides the question, the container cannot settle it; the study must widen its measurement, and possibly reopen the interface, before any system claim is made.
:::

When a change affects connections between blocks, an enclosing-boundary check must measure those integration costs. The block can remain a transfer unit for properties checked independently, while its system-power claim requires the wider measurement.

### Validating Transfer Conditions {#sec-validating-transfer-conditions}

Checks required by the transfer map establish different kinds of assurance. A formal proof establishes stated properties under specific assumptions; an equivalence check[^fn-lec-c09] establishes a defined relation between representations; deterministic analysis computes quantities under the assumptions of its model and inputs; and rule-based heuristics provide repeatability without proof of correctness. Passing target regressions supports the tool-integration behavior exercised by those tests, but does not expand formal property coverage or validate heuristic soundness (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). When a neighboring component changes a dependency relevant to the transfer claim, integration checks must cover that change even if the module itself is untouched. For example, a wrapper may parse simulator syntax correctly while receiving invalid parameters from a revised representation.

[^fn-lec-c09]: **Logic and sequential equivalence checking**: Combinational logic equivalence checking (LEC) establishes equivalence between combinational cones, often using matched registers as boundaries when comparing pre-synthesis RTL with a gate-level netlist. Retiming or changes to pipeline depth can invalidate that state correspondence. Sequential equivalence checking (SEC) instead needs a declared relation between states and observations, including any latency alignment, and a proof under the relevant environmental assumptions. Bounded model checking (BMC) can search for violations through a specified cycle depth; passing that check alone does not establish unbounded equivalence. A complete proof needs an additional argument, such as induction or a demonstrated completeness bound [@BiereEtAl1999BMC; @SymbiYosys].

Although decomposing proposal, checking, and integration into separate components makes responsibilities inspectable, that structure alone does not create independent evidence when the components share underlying models, context, training data, or tools. Distinct toolchains or information paths can expose different failures, yet shared assumptions still produce shared blind spots, so independence must be assessed for the specific property being checked (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Because component qualification does not compose automatically and localized changes often disrupt overall system behavior in ways that block-level metrics fail to detect [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden], dependency-specific checks require end-to-end integration tests wherever the claim depends on interactions between components. When evidence spans multiple fidelities, those tests must address the physical constraints relevant to the target claim before an irreversible tapeout commitment, and acting on them requires active tool access, up-to-date operating knowledge, engineer veto rights, and the instrumentation necessary to challenge anomalous tool returns (@sec-what-architect-owns).

## Transfer Under Distribution Shift {#sec-transfer-distribution-shift}

When we apply the transfer map to the array study, it exposes properties the source study left unsettled (@tbl-ch9-source-target), while moving from cycle-level simulation toward physical silicon reopens the architecture decision itself because a local no-change recommendation cannot establish that the array and its interfaces satisfy implementation constraints. In the prospective target below, each row connects a changed condition to the new obligations it creates for workload coverage, integration checks, and fallbacks; the target checks are proposed rather than executed results.

| **Condition** | **Executed array study** | **Implementation-facing target** | **Obligation created by the change** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Result cost and delay | Retained seconds-scale cycle-level simulator outputs and an inspectable replay path; no independent replay or validation result is retained | Compiler experiments (LLVM, Triton), RTL synthesis, floorplanning, and routed checks | Screening uses simulators (SCALE-Sim, gem5, Verilator) and budgets for slower downstream checks and review time. |
| Reversibility | A simulated shape can be discarded | An array and interface freeze creates downstream software and hardware rework | The 32 by 32 array remains provisional with a preserved fallback until target checks settle. |
| Coupling and interface span | Array dimensions varied while mapping and interfaces stayed fixed | Compiler mapping, RVV extensions, SRAM, NPU dataflow interconnect, host, and accelerator contracts interact | Measure the executable software path alongside end-to-end offload cost. |
| Observability and check independence | Cycles, utilization, and modeled word traffic from one simulator | Correctness, latency, bandwidth, area, timing, congestion, power, thermal behavior, reliability, and security properties required by the target | Add memory-system, RTL, implementation, thermal, fault, and security checks where target consequences demand them, disclosing shared assumptions. |
| Consequence | A local no-change recommendation | A 3\ W subsystem commitment affecting later implementation | Replace local scores with comprehensive target criteria, explicitly stating untested properties. |
| Workload | Synthetic three-layer GEMM slice | Trace-backed spatial-tracking distribution, including tails and drift | Rebuild workload coverage rather than treating the source slice as broadly representative. |
| Software turnover | One frozen mapping and tool configuration | Compiler and runtime versions (Triton, LLVM) continue to evolve | Version hardware and software together, rerunning affected claims when snapshots update. |
: **Changed conditions accumulate test obligations.** The target study retains the source record, but cannot inherit the source conclusion. {#tbl-ch9-source-target tbl-colwidths="[20,24,26,30]"}

These obligations reflect a simple expected-loss trade-off around *false acceptance*, the mistake of freezing a transferred candidate for RTL implementation when fuller target evidence would have rejected it. The expected cost of a premature freeze is the probability of false acceptance multiplied by the cost of unwinding the commitment (reworking compiler backends, repartitioning SRAM or interconnect interfaces, or absorbing a permanent power or timing penalty). Workload mismatches, limited simulator observability, and uncalibrated proxies raise the first factor, while tight cross-layer coupling and irreversible downstream commitments amplify the second.

A workload evaluation has to separate inherent workload properties from artifacts of a single machine [@HosteEeckhout2007MICA], which means specifying trace-backed distributions, common and tail execution shapes, and versioned compiler stacks. The study must also bind mapping semantics explicitly across compiler paths (Triton grid parameters, LLVM vector bounds) and simulator configurations (SCALE-Sim, gem5). Compiler autotuners such as AutoTVM and Ansor fit their cost models to measurements taken on a particular hardware target [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor], so a tuned schedule or cost model is itself a transfer unit whose accuracy on a new target must be measured before reuse.

Moving to RTL and physical implementation changes what a check can observe and what a reversal costs. Compiler-generated tests and simulation yield behavioral evidence; formal property verification establishes properties within declared model bounds; equivalence checking verifies representation mappings without proving architectural intent; and synthesis and place-and-route produce netlists, layouts, and estimates for timing, area, and congestion. Electrothermal behavior requires dedicated analysis with workload activity, power-delivery models, packaging, and thermal boundary conditions.[^fn-electrothermal-c09] Signoff additionally requires tools, models, and checks qualified for the target process. At scaled semiconductor nodes, increasing global-wire delay relative to logic gates makes extracted post-layout verification essential [@HoMaiHorowitz2001FutureOfWires].

[^fn-electrothermal-c09]: **Electrothermal feedback**: In advanced semiconductor nodes, subthreshold leakage rises steeply with junction temperature, because it scales as $e^{-qV_{\text{th}}/(n k T)}$ and the threshold voltage itself falls as the die heats. Electrothermal analysis iteratively couples power dissipation with package thermal dissipation models to capture this positive feedback loop, verifying that local compute hotspots do not trigger destructive thermal runaway or exceed thermal design power (TDP) limits.

The target checks become easier to choose when each shift is tied to the relation it can break. Five examples connect the transfer map to concrete architectural mechanisms, from the order in which a core observes writes to the energy spent moving data between packages:

1. **Cross-ISA and memory consistency shifts.** Synchronization code often relies on memory ordering that a target ISA does not preserve, such as message passing where a producer writes a payload before setting a flag and a consumer reads the payload after observing the flag. Under a relaxed model such as RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO), preserving those relationships requires explicit synchronization [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]: for ordinary memory accesses, producer-side `fence w, w` and consumer-side `fence r, r` illustrate the ordering obligations that source-language atomics and compiler lowering must also maintain. Because the invariant is visibility of the payload once the consumer observes the flag rather than the survival of the original instruction sequence, and because RVWMO remains multi-copy atomic[^fn-multicopy-relaxed-c09] rather than permitting arbitrary write propagation, target litmus tests must exercise the specific ordering relation the module depends on.[^fn-litmus-c09]
2. **Vector architecture shifts.** While fixed-width single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) kernels often hard-code a fixed element count per iteration alongside a separate scalar cleanup path, RISC-V Vector (RVV 1.0) supports vector-length-agnostic strip-mining loops in which `vsetvli`[^fn-rvv-vsetvli-c09] selects the active element count from the remaining work and the vector configuration so that each iteration advances by the returned count across supported hardware widths [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. Because the transferable unit is the algorithm together with its lowering assumptions rather than the original machine-code loop, requalification first checks numerical behavior and boundary cases under the target vector configuration before performance measurements determine whether the adapted loop uses the target datapath efficiently.
3. **Physical transistor node shifts.** Because floorplan heuristics and wire-parasitic surrogates depend on the process libraries and metal stack used to qualify them, moving from a frontside power grid to a backside power delivery network (BSPDN)[^fn-bspdn-c09] alters where power is routed and how signal-routing tracks are shared. Even when the netlist representation or prediction architecture transfers intact, its fitted delay and congestion relationships require fresh target evidence, so a node label alone establishes neither failure nor successful transfer until predictions are compared against extracted target layouts and paired with separate power-delivery and thermal checks.
4. **Workload paradigm shifts.** Whereas dense matrix multiplication gives a systolic array regular tiles and steady spatial data reuse, mixture-of-experts workloads introduce token-dependent routing that alters effective tile sizes and work balance, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly streams the key-value (KV) cache[^fn-kvcache-c09] as tokens are generated. Because these shifts can raise memory traffic relative to arithmetic work depending on how batching, compiler mapping, and the memory hierarchy respond, the transfer check reruns representative target traces to measure utilization and bandwidth together, where low array utilization motivates revising the mapping or data-movement schedule before concluding that the array hardware itself must be replaced.
5. **Interconnect and bandwidth density shifts.** Changing physical reach changes the link model that a transferred design needs. Channel loss and SerDes[^fn-serdes-c09] equalization can increase the energy spent crossing package and board boundaries, while short die-to-die links use different signaling and packaging assumptions. Bandwidth density, energy per bit, and reach therefore need to be compared under explicit interface conditions.

[^fn-multicopy-relaxed-c09]: **Multi-copy atomicity**: Once a store is visible to any hardware thread (hart) other than the one that issued it, it is visible to all other harts. This property prevents stores from propagating out of order among observers, distinguishing relaxed memory architectures such as RVWMO from architectures with non-atomic write propagation [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA].

[^fn-litmus-c09]: **Litmus tests and memory consistency transfer**: In memory consistency, litmus tests are minimal concurrent programs designed to expose whether a microarchitecture permits specific memory-access interleavings. For example, transferring synchronization primitives from total store order (TSO) environments (such as x86) to weak memory models like RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO) requires verifying explicit fence instructions (`fence rw, rw` or `fence.tso`). In a message-passing litmus test, code that omits these fences can pass single-core unit tests in Verilator yet permit stale payload reads on a multi-core RVWMO implementation.

[^fn-rvv-vsetvli-c09]: **Vector-length agility**: In RISC-V Vector (RVV), the `vsetvli` instruction dynamically sets the active vector length ($VL$) by evaluating the requested application elements against the microarchitecture's physical vector register length ($VLEN$). This enables vector-length-agnostic strip-mining, allowing one compiled loop to run on implementations with different vector register lengths (for example, 128-bit or 1024-bit $VLEN$) without a separate scalar cleanup loop.

[^fn-bspdn-c09]: **Backside power delivery network**: An arrangement that routes power through the backside of the silicon wafer, separating the power-delivery network from frontside signal routing. Its resistance and routing benefits depend on the implemented network and device connections, and a migration to backside power can invalidate wire-parasitic surrogates fitted to a frontside-power stack.

[^fn-kvcache-c09]: **Key-value cache**: In transformer models, the key-value (KV) cache stores previously computed key and value tensors for past tokens so they do not need to be recomputed. During autoregressive generation, rereading these tensors for every new token tends to make attention memory-bandwidth bound, especially at small batch sizes, shifting the bottleneck from compute throughput toward DRAM and cache transfer rates.

[^fn-serdes-c09]: **Serializer/deserializer transceiver**: A hardware transceiver block that converts parallel on-chip data streams into high-speed serial bitstreams for transmission over lossy electrical or optical channels, and reconstructs parallel data at the receiver. Equalization circuits compensate for channel attenuation, increasing energy consumption as interconnect reach extends from package substrates to printed circuit boards.

Every interconnect boundary a design crosses carries its own physical cost, and those costs limit modular scaling. A signal that stays on one die crosses only on-chip wires and repeaters. A crossing between chiplets through a die-to-die interface such as Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) or Bunch of Wires (BoW) adds interface circuitry, adapter logic, and bump parasitics, each with its own latency and energy per bit [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec].[^fn-die-interconnect-latency-c09] Links that cross package and board boundaries, such as PCIe or NVLink, generally cost more energy per bit again because they drive longer, lossier channels. Transferring an accelerator design across packaging boundaries therefore requires accounting directly for the physical crossings that workload traffic actually traverses, using parameters for the specific links and implementations involved rather than generic figures.

[^fn-die-interconnect-latency-c09]: **Die-to-die interface overheads**: UCIe and Bunch of Wires are wide, parallel, short-reach interfaces with forwarded clocks, not long-reach serializer/deserializer links, yet each crossing still pays for transmit and receive circuits, protocol adaptation, electrostatic discharge protection, and bump capacitance. Partitioning a tightly coupled systolic array or a shared-cache coherence domain across a die boundary without charging those costs can make a monolithic performance surrogate optimistic.

While wafer-scale integration reduces chip-boundary crossings for traffic kept on the wafer, co-packaged optics (CPO) carries traffic beyond the package under its own packaging and thermal constraints; in either case, transferring an accelerator requires identifying which boundaries its workload traffic actually crosses.

An interconnect transfer check therefore begins with representative target traces that identify the traffic crossing each die, package, and board boundary. For each crossing, the evaluation measures the transferred volume and its timing, compares the resulting bandwidth demand with what the target link can sustain under the intended conditions, and states which endpoint and link components are included in the energy measurement and how bandwidth density is normalized. A proposed mapping that keeps intermediate results on a wafer, for example, must be checked both for the crossings it removes and for the input and output traffic that still leaves the wafer, because a link-level improvement supports a system-level efficiency claim only after the remaining crossings and their costs are included.

Each of these five shifts calls for a different action, and the transfer map helps choose among them without declaring every source artifact obsolete.

The measurement boundary also determines which physical conclusions a check can support. Timing closure in OpenSTA or Cadence Tempus establishes that the analyzed paths meet their timing constraints under the specified process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners and modeling assumptions.[^fn-pvt-c09] It does not independently establish dynamic $IR$-drop,[^fn-irdrop-c09] electromigration, spatial thermal hotspots, or total power under a real workload, so the thermal question the node shift raises stays open after the timing report closes. Lower reversibility then demands explicit containment (bypasses, disables, guardbands, spare cells) tested against credible failure classes before the team makes an irreversible physical commitment.

[^fn-pvt-c09]: **Operating corner transferability**: Timing closure at a declared process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corner guarantees only that analyzed paths satisfy setup and hold constraints under those modeled assumptions. Reusing a block across process nodes or packaging technologies reopens closure because worst-case timing corners (such as slow silicon at high temperature) do not bound worst-case leakage or dynamic power, which peak at fast-process, high-voltage corners.

[^fn-irdrop-c09]: **Dynamic $IR$-drop**: Transient supply-voltage collapse caused by simultaneous switching activity across dense clock cycles, governed by instantaneous current spikes ($V = L \cdot di/dt + I \cdot R$). Unlike static $IR$-drop from average resistive losses, dynamic droop degrades gate propagation delays transiently, causing intermittent timing violations that traditional static timing analysis cannot observe without workload-driven switching activity traces.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A correction must reach the physical failure"}
**The claim.** On January 31, 2011, Intel disclosed a design issue in its 6 Series chipset, code-named Cougar Point, which shipped in systems built on the Sandy Bridge processors. Intel stated that consumers could continue to use their systems with confidence while manufacturers arranged a permanent solution [@Intel2011CougarPoint].

**The gap.** The defect was physical. Intel reported that Serial ATA (SATA) ports in the chipset could degrade over time, affecting attached drives. Nothing in the shipped part could reverse that degradation, so the correction was a revised chipset: Intel stopped shipping the affected part, began manufacturing a corrected version, and estimated about \$700 million to repair and replace affected materials and systems, alongside a roughly \$300 million first-quarter revenue reduction.

**The lesson.** A containment mechanism helps only if it reaches the mechanism that fails. A proposed workaround must be checked against the physical failure class it claims to contain; when the defect lies in circuitry that no configuration or firmware path can observe or bypass, only revised silicon corrects it.
:::

## Version Dependencies and Interface Contracts {#sec-version-dependencies-contracts}

Software turnover, the last row of @tbl-ch9-source-target, can change a result even when the hardware remains fixed. The offload economics that @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales works out with the LogCA model[^fn-logca-rem-c09] relate an accelerator's break-even point to communication latency, host overhead, workload granularity, host computation, and acceleration. The host runtime and compiler determine where a workload sits relative to that point, by fusing operations into payloads large enough to amortize invocation overhead and by eliminating the off-chip intermediate allocations that pull operational intensity below the link's balance point. A transferred offload result therefore carries a compiler version inside it. Move the kernel to a target whose compiler fuses less, and the same accelerator can land on the wrong side of break-even with no hardware change at all. An isolated kernel speedup becomes a transferred result only when compiler-generated code executes on the target under a pinned toolchain, with numerics, memory-ordering semantics, ABIs, and device contracts preserved, which is why the software path is a transfer unit in its own right (@tbl-ch9-transfer-map).

[^fn-logca-rem-c09]: **LogCA offload model**: The model parameters represent Latency, Overhead, Granularity, Computational index, and Acceleration ratio. As developed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, they establish the minimum kernel granularity required to amortize communication overhead and achieve net speedup.

The version pair identifies the conditions under which a hardware–software result was measured. Changing an NPU array geometry or a compiler lowering pass can alter the executed schedule even when the source program stays fixed. Hardware microarchitecture, numerical representations, and compiler schedules evolve together across abstraction boundaries, and human-designed examples show the coupling. Memory-aware algorithmic tiling (FlashAttention [@DaoEtAl2022FlashAttention]) and narrow numerical formats (Microscaling / MX formats [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling])[^fn-mx-formats-c09] make that dependence concrete. When a candidate changes its vector register configuration or systolic tile dimensions without a matched update to compiler vectorization passes or Triton tile heuristics, execution can degrade through loop peeling and unaligned memory transactions. The result is an apparent microarchitectural regression caused by compiler misalignment. Where hardware and software are revised together, candidates and compiler lowering paths cannot be qualified in isolation; they transfer, and are requalified, as one stack. Requalification follows the affected latency, bandwidth, accuracy, or efficiency claim; a version change is a reason to inspect its dependencies, not evidence that every invariant has failed.

[^fn-mx-formats-c09]: **Microscaling formats**: Standardized by the Open Compute Project, MX formats (such as MXFP8, MXFP6, and MXFP4) group blocks of narrow elements (32 in the specification's concrete formats) that share one 8-bit power-of-two scale. The shared scale recovers dynamic range that the narrow elements lack, which lets 8-bit and smaller formats save bandwidth and storage, but execution units must apply the block scale when they combine results.

Software tuning cycles run far faster than hardware implementation checks, so a fast software result must not silently overwrite the hardware baseline it was measured against. A software result can propose a hardware revision, but the revision enters versioned target state only when it is recorded in the shared study record with both version identities and approved by the architect who owns that baseline. Software state encompasses compilers, runtimes, programming interfaces, drivers, and generated binaries; comparisons with an earlier baseline require restoring the compatible dependency versions that produced it, rather than assuming an isolated binary recreates the earlier system.

MLCommons MLPerf submissions provide a public setting in which version dependence can be examined [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. Between MLPerf Training v2.1 (November 2022) and v3.0 (June 2023), NVIDIA's submissions with eight H100-SXM5-80GB GPUs improved by different amounts across three workloads (@fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend): ratios calculated from the published MLCommons times reach $1.166\times$ for BERT, $1.084\times$ for ResNet-50, and $1.082\times$ for 3D U-Net [@MLCommons2022TrainingV21Results; @MLCommons2023TrainingV30Results]. Although NVIDIA attributes the gains to software work, including fused attention, CUDA graph capture, GEMM library improvements, and convolution kernels [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware], and the GPU model and count match across both submissions, the earlier preview record leaves clock, host-memory, and detailed software fields unspecified, so the public records alone neither verify that the complete machine was unchanged nor isolate a compiler effect.

![**H100 training results improve by different amounts across workloads.** Speedups divide published MLPerf Training v2.1 times (preview result 2.1-2091) by v3.0 times (available results 3.0-2064 for BERT and 3.0-2062 for ResNet-50 and 3D U-Net) [@MLCommons2022TrainingV21Results; @MLCommons2023TrainingV30Results]. All rows list eight H100-SXM5-80GB GPUs, so per-accelerator normalization gives the same ratios. NVIDIA attributes the gains to software optimization [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware]; incomplete preview metadata limits independent claims about whole-system identity and causal attribution.](images/fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend){#fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend width="80%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of published time-to-train ratios for eight H100-SXM5-80GB GPUs from MLPerf Training v2.1 to v3.0: BERT 1.166 times, ResNet-50 v1.5 1.084 times, and 3D U-Net 1.082 times. The earlier submission was a preview system."}

Because the BERT gain for this version pair is about 17 percent whereas the other two gains are about 8 percent, carrying the BERT ratio into either workload would overstate the observed improvement, and because the series ends in June 2023, it supplies no gain for any later version pair. The published results establish a workload-dependent change between the two submissions, while testing the software attribution would require a controlled comparison that holds workload definitions, quality targets, hyperparameters, and complete machine configurations fixed. For an architect comparing an emerging accelerator with an incumbent, the practical lesson is to retain the software history alongside the hardware specification: cumulative software engineering can shift an available system's performance and must be examined before attributing the difference to microarchitecture.

When an architect compares a generated hardware candidate running on an immature compiler backend against a production baseline that benefits from years of operator fusion, the end-to-end measurement can compare the two available systems as deployed while failing to isolate their microarchitectures. Although pinning hardware revisions and compiler snapshots identifies the configurations under test when paired with their inputs, procedures, and measurement conditions, freezing the toolchain merely preserves the hardware–software interaction rather than removing it, so microarchitectural attribution requires a further comparison that probes software effects, such as tuning both candidates under matched budgets or perturbing tile sizes to test whether one result depends on a favorable compiler schedule.

Deployment observations motivate calibration studies for subsequent hardware generations, but they cannot update surrogate models or design rules automatically, because predictive uncertainty degrades under dataset shift [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift]. Calibration studies must bind observations to shipped hardware, exact software stacks, workload cohorts, and measurement conditions, separating calibration samples from held-out validation sets. A surrogate calibrated on one software release inherits that release, so a later driver or compiler update is itself a shift that the calibration study must record.

## Cross-Stack Pattern Transfer {#sec-cross-stack-pattern-transfer}

For our Lighthouse transfer, the work maps directly onto the dependencies exposed earlier. Because the target remains prospective and the retained array sweep has not been extended into an implementation-facing study, the admission check identifies a new design problem: freezing the array and its interfaces carries consequences the source simulator score cannot assess. Once the source study is partitioned into its historical records, workload definitions, project state, proposing methods, SCALE-Sim screen, tool interfaces, candidate identities, and conclusions, the affected slice runs through nearly every dependency the target touches, from workload distributions and compiler mappings to process libraries, physical checks, and the power target. As a result, the source simulator outputs survive as historical data without supplying implementation evidence; the team can preserve those historical artifacts while rebuilding the workload and project state, requalifying the screen against target references, and keeping the source recommendation confined to its original scope. Each changed dependency then pairs with a target check that can observe its risk, and any claimed benefit from carrying the source material forward still requires a matched target-only arm.

The test structures the study but does not authorize an array or interface freeze; until legal target candidate sets and credible comparators are declared, the target decision remains open.

Two units illustrate why the assigned actions differ. While the SCALE-Sim wrapper and the five candidate identities can be retained for reuse, a pending rerun under the pinned source configuration would test only whether the wrapper reproduces the retained cycle and utilization counts, qualifying source-study execution rather than the wrapper's ability to predict Lighthouse power.

The source decision rule has a different limit. Its ratio of cycles to utilization omits the memory traffic that the simulator also modeled (@sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration in @sec-feedback-verification-trust). Word traffic matters to the target because moving each word consumes energy, but traffic counts alone do not establish power.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Derived, not measured: energy of the extra modeled DRAM writes of the 16 x 64 candidate.
# Inputs:
#   extra writes   data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json
#   pJ per access  data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv, "DRAM access, 64 bit" (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm)
# Assumption: each modeled word costs one full 64-bit DRAM access.
# The target execution rate is unknown; no other traffic, refresh, or interface energy is counted.
import csv as _csv9e
import json as _json9e
from pathlib import Path as _Path9e
import _python.plots as _ap9e

_root9e = _Path9e(_ap9e.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_st9e = _json9e.loads((_root9e / "data" / "studies" / "ai_systolic_array_study" / "recorded" / "reference" / "study_results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_m9e = {e["candidate_id"]: e["metrics"] for e in _st9e["evaluations"]}
_extra9e = _m9e["ai_wide_16x64"]["dram_writes"] - _m9e["model_baseline_32x32"]["dram_writes"]
with open(_root9e / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _dram9e = next(r for r in _csv9e.DictReader(_fh) if r["operation_or_access"] == "DRAM access")
_pj_lo9e, _pj_hi9e = float(_dram9e["energy_low_pj"]), float(_dram9e["energy_high_pj"])
_mj_lo9e = _extra9e * _pj_lo9e * 1e-9
_mj_hi9e = _extra9e * _pj_hi9e * 1e-9
en_extra_writes = f"{_extra9e:,}"
en_pj_lo = f"{_pj_lo9e / 1000:.1f}"
en_pj_hi = f"{_pj_hi9e / 1000:.1f}"
en_mj_lo = f"{_mj_lo9e:.3f}"
en_mj_hi = f"{_mj_hi9e:.3f}"
```

A derived estimate makes the missing quantities explicit. The $16 \times 64$ candidate issues `{python} en_extra_writes` more modeled DRAM-word writes per pass of the workload slice than the baseline. If each extra word costs one full 64-bit access, its additional write energy and average power are

$$
\Delta E_{\mathrm{writes}} = \Delta N_{\mathrm{writes}} E_{\mathrm{access}},
\qquad
\Delta P_{\mathrm{writes}} = \Delta E_{\mathrm{writes}} f_{\mathrm{slice}},
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{slice}}$ is the number of slice executions per second. Substituting the historical `{python} en_pj_lo` to `{python} en_pj_hi`\ nJ per 64-bit access reported by @Horowitz2014Energy gives `{python} en_mj_lo` to `{python} en_mj_hi`\ mJ per pass under that assumption, although the word count is a simulator return and the energy anchor is source-transcribed without direct measurement on Lighthouse. Because that historical anchor reflects an older process node and memory interface, while charging a full access per word overstates energy whenever narrower words are packed into bursts and the target execution rate $f_{\mathrm{slice}}$ remains unknown, testing the 3\ W constraint requires a calibrated energy model, measured execution rates, and the rest of the subsystem power budget before the source score can admit any array shape for implementation, including the retained 32 by 32 reference.

An automated transfer harness that carries the source comparator forward could incorrectly describe the reference array as power-qualified, producing an unsupported power conclusion rather than a demonstrated 3\ W violation. Because a memory-aware target comparison might retain that array, choose another, or reject every candidate, keeping those outcomes open is what permits the source artifacts to help without letting the source verdict decide a different problem.

Reuse also need not freeze the source design space into an immutable container $\Theta$. If target constraints showed that the array template itself was the obstacle, the study would have to leave parameter search and reopen the organization, whether through conventional redesign or through an AI-native design system qualified to revise several layers together (such as software loop schedules and explicit memory structures like software-managed scratchpads) under extracted timing, dynamic $IR$-drop, and electrothermal analysis in the 3\ nm-class target process. No such system has been qualified for this study, and neither route is presumed to succeed; either would face the same matched-baseline test, establish its own mapping, memory-interface, and implementation checks, and remain subject to target signoff obligations regardless of whether the source simulator wrapper is retained.

Target obligations pair minimum tests with explicit claim boundaries (@tbl-ch9-target-tests), and an obligation left untested stays out of every generalized claim.

| **Target obligation** | **Minimum test** | **Boundary if absent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Workload coverage** | Trace-backed common and tail cases, strictly versioned with all exclusions declared. | No representativeness claim. |
| **Candidate comparison** | Predeclared legal target space, search/evaluation budgets, credible comparator, decision rule, and sensitivity check. | No claims outside evaluated candidates; no comparative AI-contribution claim if arms cannot be distinguished. |
| **Transfer benefit** | Matched comparison against a target-only arm sharing tasks, data, tool access, budgets, and stopping rules, accounting for adaptation, requalification, integration, and retirement costs. | Forfeit transfer-benefit claim. Harmful priors must be retired; cost-neutral priors retained only if improving another declared criterion. |
| **Mapping and software path** | Compiler-generated end-to-end execution with a declared, supported backend for each path (such as LLVM/RVV, or Triton where a target backend is available), using pinned mappings, compilers, runtimes, ISA configurations, and interfaces. | Cannot claim array is usable by the target software stack. |
| **Interface and memory cost** | Measure offload granularity, bandwidth, traffic, and latency on the target or a qualified reference path; use LogCA and Roofline to interpret performance limits, with calibrated energy models capturing execution rates, duty cycles, leakage, and subsystem boundaries. | Forfeit 3\ W power or system-speedup claims. |
| **Cheap-screen validity** | Check representative target samples against a reference able to observe the screened property, enforcing class-specific error limits, uncertainty measures, and drift audits. Models such as gem5 or Verilator may support functional or cycle-level checks within their scope; physical and energy claims need suitable implementation or calibrated energy references. | SCALE-Sim serves as a source study tool rather than a valid target decision filter. |
| **RTL behavior** | Independently derived reference tests, linting, functional simulation (Verilator), synthesis (Yosys), formal property verification (JasperGold / SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)), and target-specific fault/threat models. | No implementation-readiness, reliability, or security claims beyond checked properties. |
| **Physical behavior** | Pin the 3\ nm-class low-power process design kit (PDK), foundry-compiled SRAM macros, standard cell libraries, and PVT corners. At advanced nodes such as the 3\ nm class, select commercial implementation and signoff suites (such as Synopsys Fusion Compiler/PrimeTime or Cadence Innovus/Tempus) rather than academic trailing-node flows (such as OpenROAD/OpenSTA); check setup/hold corners, congestion, design rule check (DRC), layout versus schematic (LVS), dynamic $IR$-drop, electromigration, and electrothermal behavior with qualified analysis flows (such as Synopsys RedHawk-SC Electrothermal). | No physical-feasibility claim beyond checked conditions. Signoff and tapeout require a separately qualified foundry flow. |
| **Containment** | Exercise bypasses, disable functions, guardbands, isolation mechanisms, and fallbacks against specific target faults or attacks. | Cannot claim implementation will contain or recover from failure. |
| **Operational readiness** | Confirm tool access, engineer veto rights and instrumentation to challenge anomalous tool returns, and recorded decision authority. | Cannot claim transferred workflow is operable, challengeable, or capable of supporting commitment. |
: **Target obligations define required measurements.** Untested boundaries remain explicit in the architectural record. {#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[25,45,30]"}

The cheap-screen row separates executable reuse from predictive validity. A cheap screen such as SCALE-Sim transfers as an empirical check, never as a verdict. Its validated coverage on the target, the share of comparisons it settles within declared error against a reference that can observe the property at risk, is measured anew, and the screening economics that @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization works out apply only to that target-measured coverage.

The same test applies well beyond the array across learned, software, and physical artifacts (@tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests). A learned congestion predictor of the kind evaluated with CircuitNet [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet] carries its fitted relationships into a new process only after target requalification, just as ChiPBench evaluates placement algorithms on their final power, performance, and area rather than treating an intermediate proxy metric as the outcome [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench].
